body_paragraphs: REVON: LOG AND MERKLE DIFFERENCING FOR DURABLE STRUCTURED DATA VERSIONING

By Atharva Sheersh Pandey1,a, Adhyan Jain1,b,
and Poornima Nedunchezhian1,c
1 School of Computer Science and Engineering, VIT Vellore
a atharva.sheersh2024@vitstudent.ac.in; b adhyan.jain2024@vitstudent.ac.in
c Corresponding author: Poornima Nedunchezhian (poornima.n@vit.ac.in)

Revon is a Python implementation of a key/value Merkle hash trie history, implemented on top of a SQLite database. We employ it for comparing log aggregation versus hash pruned diffing on one history, testing an operation-count based selection policy and measuring full versioning processes. For the Linux experiment, 516 runs come with an additional set of 72 runs geometry and telemetry information. In eight of nine timing comparison intervals for the hybrid/Merkle pairing, hybrid wins; the dense interval also includes parity. An additional threshold control shows a slower alternative: the policy selects Merkle if log is faster. The Windows experiment consists of 93 trials, each done in a new process, using disjoint sets of calibration and validation histories. It consists of controlled sensitivity analysis, Wine Quality and CO2 data sources, and repeated runs with 100,000 and 1,000,000 records. The winner of the calibration round uses log on every considered interval, so these results do not allow for concluding on the advantage of the switch. The CO2 histories include observed publication updates; wine corrections are artificial. Diff and historical state correctness are confirmed by semantic oracles; algorithmic, command line interface phase and full-process measurements are separated.

1. Introduction.  An application that maintains dataset versions should be able to restore previous versions and determine the differences between them. Maintaining a full backup for each version partially solves this problem; however, the application also has to track and compare history at the record level. Git is known to use content-addressable objects for file history, where the content of objects uniquely identifies objects, and commits link parent objects [10]. These objects represent files and directories. Record history poses another issue. Keys could remain identical while updates are made more or less often.

We fix the history representation and compare two methods to traverse to its endpoint changes. The first method uses the operations recorded in the log, whereas the second compares Merkle hashes and skips identical subtrees. The two methods yield the same semantic difference starting from the same representation. To facilitate such comparison, we integrate existing techniques of path copying and content addressing with SQLite transaction model. Moreover, we estimate the effectiveness of a rule to choose which of the two paths to take. Timings include all versioning operations and data workloads considered in this work.

Other systems provide the context for such comparison. Dolt merges SQL database with commit graph and Prolly trees [13, 28]; ForkBase is an implementation of fork-aware database management system with POS-Tree and SIRI storage structure [32]; Noms describes history independent chunked collections [3]. Revon exposes key-value operations against a linear history to enable diff path comparison in a controlled manner. Such scope does not imply equivalence to feature sets of the aforementioned systems or introduction of new persistent indexes family. For cross-system measurements In our study, we employ Revon through its in-process API and Dolt through its CLI, separately recording the phases of the CLI for the clear boundaries of the comparison.

1.1. Research Questions.  RQ1: What is the relationship between latency, persistent storage, and worker resources in versioning workflows, and how does the API/CLI distinction affect these measurements?
RQ2: How well does the selection of the paths by operation count succeed on generated histories not seen during calibration, compared to forced log and forced Merkle?
RQ3: Under experimental variations of tested histories, how do workload structure, payload size and fixed-trie geometry affect the cost of differencing?

1.2. Contributions.  Our implementation uses atomic SQLite-based persistence, content addressing and path copying in the prototype consisting of two diff paths, both following the single contract for the encoded value. This integration and comparison of the paths under matched conditions represent the engineering contribution.

For the path selection we design a simple rule based on operation count and compare its choices with the forced execution of the paths. We complete the calibration process and register the selection threshold prior to testing on the held-out histories. Those cases when the selection takes more time than the paths execution are part of the analysis, as well as the question about using the log for all of the histories.

The verification evidence is based on the comparison of the observed diffs and historical states to the oracles constructed independently from the storage implementation. The executed sources, the raw measurements, the environment configuration and data preparation procedures are attached with the paper. This also includes the description of the correctness checks performed and what is measurable by the telemetry.

We provide the results of the Linux workflow experiments along with 93 case Windows evaluation campaign. In our Windows setup, validation seeds are distinct from calibration seeds; matched sensitivity control, Wine Quality and CO2 sources, multiple scales runs extend the comparison. Since each experiment employs a different experimental unit, each campaign is analyzed separately, and their timing rows are separated.

The evidence scope is limited by the single writer store, linear histories and the tested workloads. It can provide the trade-offs in these conditions. It cannot determine the universal best selector and geometry, prove query engine superiority or reproduce with another team independently.
2. Related Work.

2.1. Content Addressing and Persistent Structures.  A collection authenticated using its Merkle root can be authenticated using that root [22]. Content-addressing allows software history in Git and IPFS in the case of networked content [10, 5]. Persistent data structures use path-copying to keep old versions and share the unchanged parts of the data structure [14]. Ordered stratified B-trees [31] and fully persistent B-trees [8] solve disk-based dictionary problems. Revon employs an alternative routing technique, where hashes are passed to a fixed-depth trie. Matching hashes can stop a comparison but cannot be used for an ordered range search. SciDB and TimeArr are designed for versioned arrays having layouts and deltas designed specifically for arrays [27, 30]. TardisDB provides versioned accesses in main memory, and Saquib et al. study replicated versioned data structures in wide area networks [25, 26]. These designs may give us some clues about the design decisions made in Revon, but they do not cover the comparison between the log and Merkle paths of Revon in the same history.

Merkle Search Trees resolve states by merging search tree ordering and Merkle authentication [4]. In Revon, search is pruned by hash, but the routing strategy is fixed-depth, and history is linear and central as opposed to replicated CRDT. LBFS detects redundant content based on content-defined chunking [23]; there are other chunk boundary techniques in Dolt and Noms. Chunk boundaries allow for deduplication during movement of data and ordered indexes for range searches. Neither of them is covered in Revon benchmark.

2.2. Structured Dataset Versioning.  A system for dataset-versioning needs to enable collaboration in addition to state persistence and reconstruction. DataHub explores collaborative histories at scale [6]. Decibel facilitates relational branching using version-first, tuple-first and hybrid representations [20]. OrpheusDB relies on partitioning to enhance version lookup if an already extant DBMS becomes capable of versioning [19]. The storage-reconstruction dilemma is addressed by Bhattacherjee et al. [7]. Delta Lake creates ACID-compliant tables via transactions logs and checkpoints [2] while the version graph approach picks materialized versions and deltas under storage and retrieval constraints [18]. FAIR-compliance related problems of release naming and description are the topic of the FAIR-compliant proposal [16], which adds to the current storage research without providing any diff algorithm. 2.4. Design Implications and Research Positioning.  Representation choices move work between version creation, retention, reconstruction and comparison. A complete snapshot is easy to retrieve but copies unchanged records. A log leaves work for replay or checkpointing. With path copying, the unchanged structure is shared and only update-affected paths are rebuilt [14, 7]. Decibel and OrpheusDB show how layout affects version creation and retrieval [20, 19], and version-graph analyses make the storage/retrieval trade-off explicit [18]. Reproducibility research considers how builds and artifacts can be kept available for inspection [1]. We therefore report import, commit, checkout, diff and storage separately. Retaining an artifact enables inspection; it is not evidence that the implementation runs faster.

Different studies also mean different things by a change. Differential dataflow updates query results when timestamped inputs change [21]. Provenance describes the origins of output facts and why those facts occur [9]. DSLog captures fine-grained array lineage and supports queries over it [33]. Explain-Da-V relates semantic dataset changes to transformations [29], while Baseline uses operation-based differencing for refactorings and schema changes [15]. Revon restricts its output to keys added, removed or modified between two states. Causes, lineage, effects on queries and schema intent are not inferred. The related studies provide context, but their workloads and outputs are too different to support direct timing comparisons with these key/value diffs.

Each Revon-H commit retains both a content-addressed changeset and a Merkle root, allowing either path to recover the same endpoint changes. The selection rule changes how the diff is computed. We expect log aggregation to suit short, sparse intervals and hypothesize that hash pruning may help after longer sequences of operations; whether their costs cross has to be measured. Git4Data shows the wider interest in database-native version control [17]. For our fixed-depth-trie comparison, Snapshot and Log-only serve as representation baselines. The public workloads consist of generated TLC and wine corrections and observed changes in a CO2 publication sequence. Their results do not establish performance across independent hardware, concurrent workloads or production systems.

3. Revon Design.  Figure 1 shows the implemented architecture and places the evaluated operations within it.
Fig 1. Revon architecture showing the implemented scope of the research prototype

3.1. Addressed Object Model.  Revon names a trie node or changeset by the SHA-256 digest of its canonical JSON serialization. The digest for a commit includes the root, parent, changeset, message and timestamp. Human-readable names such as v1 and v2 are aliases and do not affect object identity. The current commit is identified by a durable HEAD reference.

3.2. Fixed-Depth Merkle Hash Trie.  For the main configuration, b=8 and d=4. Each routing level consumes three bits of SHA-256(key), giving twelve bits that select one of 4,096 possible leaf buckets. Leaves retain complete keys, so keys sharing a routing prefix remain distinguishable. Expected occupancy under uniform hashing is N/b^d. Other b,d combinations are evaluated separately; we do not assume the default minimizes cost.

3.3. Incremental Hashing and Commit.  A batch is processed by canonicalizing its values and grouping keys with the same routing prefix. Revon rewrites each touched leaf once, then rebuilds the ancestors on the affected paths. Unchanged child hashes remain in internal nodes, sharing the structure beneath them. The objects, changeset, commit metadata, version alias and measurements are written and HEAD is updated in a single SQLite transaction. Reopening the repository checks stored payload hashes and references.

3.4. Hybrid Diff.  Log differencing composes operations by key while traversing the requested ancestor interval. Merkle differencing compares roots recursively, stops when hashes match and examines entries beneath unequal paths. Revon-H validates the version identifiers, checks ancestry in both directions and counts changeset operations before selecting a path. Log is used for an eligible ancestor interval whose count is no greater than T; otherwise selection goes to Merkle. A reverse log request exchanges old and new values, while a request comparing a version with itself returns an empty diff. Forced log rejects unrelated versions. Unknown identifiers raise an error. Revon-M always requests Merkle, with ancestry still checked by its public version-pair API. Both paths produce the same sorted semantic diff, and commit and checkout are timed independently.

The Linux workflow protocol sets T=4,096. For a separate Linux control, an auxiliary calibration experiment selected T=16,384. T measures operation count, whereas b^d determines bucket capacity. Neither parameter was fitted to the Linux results.

3.5. JSON value ownership and identity.  Revon accepts JSON nulls, booleans, finite numbers, strings, lists and objects with string keys. Input containers are validated and detached before storage, and containers returned through reads or diagnostic views are detached too. Immutable scalars may be shared. Before writing, Revon rejects unsupported Python values, nested non-string keys, non-finite numbers and cyclic containers. Its v1 JSON encoding defines equality through sorted object keys, compact separators, UTF-8 and the exclusion of NaN. The encodings of true, 1, 1.0 and signed floating zero remain distinct. These requirements describe the encoding contract of the Python prototype, without asserting compliance to the canonical-JSON encoding of cross-language JSON.

Algorithm 1 (batch update). Start by verifying the batch and claiming the values. Prior to interning an object, reject keys appearing in both puts and deletes, and requests to delete non-existent keys. Read the old values and keep the mutations if the encoded identity has changed. Group the mutations by routing prefix, reconstruct each affected leaf and sort its entries and hash the entire payload. Recreate the affected ancestors with the unmodified child hashes wherever possible. Log the content-addressed changeset and commit. Detaching values stops users from changing history through their input containers and read operations.

Algorithm 2 (log composition). Scan the ancestor interval chronologically. For each key, keep its existence and value at the earliest old and latest new endpoints. Remove it from the results if the two endpoints have equal existence and value. The insertion followed by deletion cancels out, as does the update followed by restoration. Null is different from non-existence. Sort the keys left in the results; reverse requests switch endpoints and the added/deleted labels.

Algorithm 3 (selection). Verify the version pair and check whether one is an ancestor of the other. Sum the operation counts of changesets in the interval. Pick the log if the interval is valid and the sum is less than or equal to T; otherwise pick the Merkle tree. Merkle traversal skips the trees with equal hashes and compares values in the unequal leaves. Apply the encoded identity test to both, detach values returned to the caller.

Cost model. Let N be the record count, d the depth and b the branching factor. Write m for the keys in a batch, h for interval length, p for accumulated operations, u for distinct keys in the interval and s for serialized output bytes. Expected leaf occupancy is N/(b^d) with uniform routing, but can reach N in the worst case. Besides validating and copying inputs, a batch performs m routed old-value lookups and scans occupied leaves. It sorts and serializes touched leaves and copies affected internal child maps. This work prevents a dataset-independent O(d) bound for batch processing.

Log composition traverses ancestry with O(p + u log u) work, plus the costs of encoded-value comparison and output copying/serialization. Merkle cost depends on the visited nodes pair, child-slot sorting, and leaves examined. Value comparison and output sorting also contribute to Merkle cost. In both public version-pair modes, Merkle tree ancestry traversal takes place. If the request is reversed, the unsuccesssful direction will revert to genesis first. Construction of the output will take at least linear time of s. Comparison and copying of large JSON values require additional cost than the benchmark of scalar value can provide.

Retained nodes, changeset, and commit are read eagerly from the SQLite database. Even if they are durable on the disk, they are kept in memory as long as Revon runs; thus, retained history needs to be able to fit in memory. Retained payload will affect the performance of repository open and validation process. No disk page caching or eviction strategy is included in this prototype.

7. Discussion.  The workflow measurements answer Research Question 1 (RQ1) at the application interface. Measurements for import, commit, diff, checkout, and persistent footprint have been gathered in both the Linux and Windows experiments. Rows per campaign are considered individually. Both the snapshot and Log-only settings demonstrate representation costs; while the forced M, H, and log comparisons fix Revon’s representation. Dolt provides a richer SQL/versioning interface. The separation into discrete command phases enables us to investigate the workflow without mixing it with tree operations and a standalone Python call.

Research Question 2 (RQ2) explores if the parameter selected for one set of histories can be applied to other sets of histories. In the Windows split, the primary parameters (N, H, payload, and geometry) will remain constant and the selection will be recorded prior to the validation phase. The largest candidate in this case is the always-log setting within the measured parameter space. Parity in dense cases and the unfavorable Linux threshold selection show why taking the fastest route is not possible. More sophisticated selection would require independent calibration followed by untainted measurement. No grounds for changing the default threshold have been found here.

Research Question 3 (RQ3) demonstrates that equal capacity does not necessarily result in identical traversal depths and costs of ancestor reconstruction even if the expected occupancy is identical with uniform routing. Payload encoding, leaf inspection, and output construction add time to the latency. Seeds are independently generated in the Windows cases with the controls, while the Linux geometry uses a single history. Neither configuration models all interactions nor finds the optimum for a population.

Consistent value semantics are necessary for diff comparison. Detached input and output of Revon prevent mutable aliases from affecting history retention. The v1 encoded identity value true is distinct from 1, 1 is distinct from 1.0, and object encoding and the on-disk schema is unchanged. The Linux test exercises these semantics against provided histories. Unit tests check for null vs. absence, nested ownership, unsupported values, and rollback.

8. Limitations And Future Work.  External Validity: The Linux campaign was run on a single cloud virtual machine, whereas the Windows manifest was done on a single local machine, both controlled by the authors. Such setups cannot be considered independent party replications or operating system comparison. There are a number of co-variables associated with hardware, runtime, virtualization, and storage properties. Caches and background services were enabled and the Windows manifest reports limited amount of RAM available and process status. This study does not capture idle host or cold caches.

Workload Validity: TLC histories were generated with updates to one monthly release. Linux scale diagnostic runs are n=1 per system. The Windows validation uses three generated seed per primary profile, generated wine corrections and one observed CO2 publication sequence. Three CO2 repositories use the same sequence of events instead of generating independent histories. Header-only revisions are trimmed before timing, whereas unnamed columns are kept but are not scientifically analyzed. The synthetic scale histories are sampled from a common distribution. Broader generalization would require other domains, observations and hardware.

Implementation Scope: Revon trie uses a fixed geometry, eagerly loading the retained nodes, changesets and commits, without eviction. The fixed-geometry trie implementation supports single writer and linear history. The evaluation does not consider named branches, merge commits, conflict resolution, schema evolution, remote connections, ordered scans, crash faults injection or concurrent execution. The atomic SQLite transactions alone are not sufficient proof of all durability guarantees required for production.

Measurement and Inference: Dolt command time measures the whole process execution time, including native computations and JSON emission. Worker RSS measure includes oracle and history state. Sampling interval of ten milliseconds may miss the process peak or even process. Windows I/O counters measure neither physical disk usage nor database logical reads and the comparison between sampler on/off conditions confuse order and caching. Linux bootstrap time captures repeated timings of fixed histories. Windows three-history timings represent descriptive statistics and not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Checks of sources and semantic hashes are used for internal self-consistency, but not timing repeatability checks.

Selection and Design: the first Windows calibration examines four threshold settings, two starting seeds, and the selected profiles. Its highest test candidate, T=65,536, never switches in the selected test range, leaving the potential benefits of broader selection-based adaptation unclear. The sensitivity design is partial rather than full-factorial: for constant operations H is compared to density, and in hash route tests the appropriate low density control must be used. Another selection mechanism or crossover would require a separate constant experiment.

Future storage enhancements may involve binary nodes, object values, packed objects, data compression, and reachability-based garbage collection. An ordered Merkle index or content-driven chunking can facilitate a range operations alternative approach. Each change requires semantic and performance testing; the results for fixed tries cannot predict their influence.

9. Conclusion.  Revon offers two semantically coherent diff paths on a content-addressed, fixed-trie history stored atomically in SQLite. The contribution represents an inspectable prototype supported by empirical evaluations of workflow and selection costs. Linux-based results include 516 executions supplemented with 72 executions and cover the dense case result in question, along with the negative threshold selection choice. Windows-based results consist of 93 worker tests and 3,402 query tests performed on held-out histories, Wine Quality and CO2 data sets, interface phases, and scaled runs. The tuned policy with T = 65,536 applies log all through the observed primary matrix, leaving the best crossover point still unknown. The documented workloads demonstrate conditional trade-offs, limited by the restrictions of API/CLI usage, sampling, data set, and hardware. These do not confirm a universal speed benefit and do not allow for independent reproduction of the results.

APPENDIX B: METHODS AND EVIDENCE DETAILS

Linux tarballs keep the sources that have been executed, along with their hashes, environments, fixed workloads, order of execution, observations, and audit trail. The workers start with PYTHONHASHSEED=20261008. Preflight runs 67 unit tests for the main and 69 for the supplemental campaign before measurement. The preflight of the supplemental campaign reports an incomplete data transfer due to a missing test_data directory. After the fixture directory is restored, the entire test suite runs successfully before the time measurements start. In case of setup failure, the execution logs keep the record.

Each run of the main campaign creates a repository in the new worker. Deterministic shuffling and rotation decide on the order of models within each repetition block. Import timings stop on the first durable version. The median of individual commit timers gives the incremental commit latency of a particular history. Diff produces the comparison of the initial and final versions in the form of sorted changed keys with their old/new values' hashes in canonical JSON format. The checkout writes the entire sorted key-value state in canonical UTF-8 JSON. The Revon engine is run using in-process API; Dolt timings include the invocation of the command line interface, JSON parsing, and output normalization. Therefore, workflow ratios cannot be compared in terms of the speed of engines.

Correctness verification is excluded from the operation timings. For each run of the main campaign, we verify the initial and final state hashes, all H+1 historical states, and the observed canonical diff against the workload oracle built separately. Verification logs include the expected and observed hashes. Audit checks regenerate workloads, check matrix membership, selected paths and source/data/protocol identities, and compute summaries. Downloaded logs are audited too. These checks guarantee internal integrity, not the independent replication of the timing experiment.

The medians and IQRs of latency for the seven examined repository trials after excluding the warm-up period are presented below. The latency ratios are calculated by comparing the matched pairs of the trials. For each pair of trials, the ratio's median value and paired percentile-bootstrap confidence interval with 20,000 bootstrap resamples are reported. A ratio higher than one implies preference for the denominator. The exploratory 95% confidence intervals refer to repeated timing of the same workload on one virtual machine and are neither representative of population effect nor adjusted for multiple comparisons. The median of paired ratios does not coincide with the ratio of latency medians. All finished trials are kept; timing outliers are included too.

In order to sample the resident set size (RSS), CPU utilization, and I/O usage of the worker process and its descendents, the parent process collects information every 10 milliseconds. In addition to storage operations, peaks contain information about workload creation, oracle state, and verification. Therefore, it is impossible to attribute the whole peak to the storage engine. Short-lived subprocesses or temporary peaks can be observed between samples. The main Linux sampler considers a fully zero read counter to be unavailable data and cannot provide any information about read I/O. The second campaign distinguishes measured zeros and unavailable counters, so it is analyzed separately. Cached bytes can be logically analyzed while physical read bytes are zero.

The Linux footprint measure represents the directory size before the closure and compaction. It also includes indexes, metadata, and representation cost. Logical-payload normalization and compaction probes of the first trial are included in the measurements. The measurements relate to the complete workflow and not just tree overhead. CPU, RSS, and I/O measurements cover the whole life cycle of the worker process and last longer than operation timers.

In the auxiliary Windows threshold experiment, the calibration and validation profiles are pre-defined and non-overlapping. Possible candidate values of T are 1,024, 2,048, 4,096, 8,192, and 16,384 operations. The minimization of normalized calibration latency leads to the selection of T = 16,384 prior to validation, resulting in a held-out normalized score of 1.032 compared to 1.297 for T = 4,096. The always-log scores are 1.000 in both splits. The cached-query data correspond to the recorded source and environment of the experiment and are distinct from Linux measurements. One largest-candidate winner does not form an optimum. Long-horizon history and three seeds pilot create the exploratory setting.

Linux threshold control uses a fixed value of T = 16,384 with 10,000 rows and 512 changes per commit. Values H = 16 and H = 64 lead to 8,192 and 32,768 operations, respectively. Forced log, forced Merkle, and hybrid configurations run separately, each using two warm-up runs and seven measured trials. The threshold is not based on Linux results. abstract: Revon is a Python implementation of a key/value Merkle hash trie history, implemented on top of a SQLite database. We employ it for comparing log aggregation versus hash pruned diffing on one history, testing an operation-count based selection policy and measuring full versioning processes. For the Linux experiment, 516 runs come with an additional set of 72 runs geometry and telemetry information. In eight of nine timing comparison intervals for the hybrid/Merkle pairing, hybrid wins; the dense interval also includes parity. An additional threshold control shows a slower alternative: the policy selects Merkle if log is faster. The Windows experiment consists of 93 trials, each done in a new process, using disjoint sets of calibration and validation histories. It consists of controlled sensitivity analysis, Wine Quality and CO2 data sources, and repeated runs with 100,000 and 1,000,000 records. The winner of the calibration round uses log on every considered interval, so these results do not allow for concluding on the advantage of the switch. The CO2 histories include observed publication updates; wine corrections are artificial. Diff and historical state correctness are confirmed by semantic oracles; algorithmic, command line interface phase and full-process measurements are separated.
